## The CAPA record nobody can find

Three weeks after the planning meeting that closed out the last module, you're sitting in a
follow-up with your Quality Analyst and your systems administrator, and she asks a question that
stops the conversation cold: "If someone altered a CAPA (corrective and preventive action) record
in the eQMS (electronic quality-management system) after it was closed — changed the stated root
cause, say, or the effectiveness-check date — would we actually know?"

Nobody answers right away. Your systems administrator finally says, "Probably not, unless someone
happened to notice." Your QA follows with a worse one: "And if Brookfield's site lead can see
Fairview's open CAPA records before they're ready to share — is that a problem?" Then the one that
really lands: "What if an AABB assessor shows up the week the eQMS is down for a migration and
asks for the audit log on a specific deviation? What do we hand them?"

Three questions, three different ways the eQMS could fail, and none of them is "the system
crashes." That's exactly the gap you went looking for a framework to close. You decided, in the
last module, to run the eQMS through RMF's (Risk Management Framework's) structure, start to
finish, as Lakeshore's own voluntary methodology. This is the session where that decision stops
being theoretical. Categorize comes first — and categorize is just a formal name for the three
questions your QA and your administrator just asked, asked on purpose instead of by accident.

## Why this step exists — and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure Categorize is built to prevent: a team picks controls for a system before
anyone has agreed on what the system is actually worth protecting, which means the controls end
up sized to whoever argued loudest in the room, not to the system's actual stakes. Skip
straight to "what controls should we put on the eQMS" without Categorize, and you get one of two
bad outcomes — either the systems administrator's instinct to lock everything down as tightly as
possible (expensive, slow, and probably still wrong in some other direction), or his instinct from
the last module to "keep an eye on it" (cheap, fast, and wrong in the direction that actually
matters). Categorize forces the sizing question to happen first, out loud, on the record.

You already know this motion from ITSM (IT service management): it's the same discipline behind
**service classification** in a service catalog — deciding a service is Tier 1 versus Tier 3 before
you decide its incident-response SLA (service-level agreement), its change-approval rigor, or its
monitoring depth. Nobody writes a four-hour-restore SLA for every service in the catalog
regardless of what it does; the tiering decision comes first, and it drives everything after it.
Categorize is that tiering decision, asked three specific ways — confidentiality, integrity,
availability — instead of one generic "how important is this."

One callback before you go further, because it matters every time this course touches RMF: nothing
here is a federal requirement. RMF is written for U.S. federal information systems; Lakeshore is
borrowing its structure voluntarily, the same way it borrowed AABB's accreditation structure and
ICH Q9's. The eQMS will never receive an actual federal "authorization to operate." What follows is
Lakeshore's own disciplined use of a well-built framework, not compliance with anything that binds
a private blood establishment.

## The rule in plain English

Categorize asks one question, three ways, about a system before you touch a single control:
**if this system's data loses confidentiality, integrity, or availability, how bad does that
actually get for the organization?** Not "is the eQMS important" — everything feels important in
the room where you're deciding its budget. The question is sharper: name the three specific ways
it could fail, and reason out loud about how bad each one is, separately, before picking a single
control.

Applied to your QA's three questions from the opening scene:

- **Integrity** — a CAPA record altered after closure, undetected. The root-cause finding and
  effectiveness-check date are exactly the fields an AABB assessor or an FDA investigator would
  rely on to judge whether Lakeshore actually fixed what it said it fixed. An undetected change
  doesn't just corrupt a record — it corrupts the evidence Lakeshore would use to defend a closed
  CAPA at the next reassessment.
- **Confidentiality** — an open CAPA record visible to someone at another site before it's ready
  to share. CAPA records routinely discuss an employee's error, a near-miss, or a vendor problem
  before root cause is confirmed. Premature or unrestricted visibility across three sites isn't
  just an awkward conversation; it's exactly the kind of access-control gap your systems
  administrator was worried about from day one, just named specifically now instead of generally.
- **Availability** — the eQMS down, or a specific audit log unreachable, the week an assessor asks
  for it. "We'll pull that up once the system's back" is not an answer an assessor accepts on the
  spot, and a document-control or audit-log system that can't produce a record on demand is close
  to useless for the exact purpose it exists for.

## Citation decoder

Same citation shape as last module — a document number and revision, then a chapter and section
number, read the way you'd read any numbered technical document.

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, §3.2 (Categorize's purpose) | "Special Publication eight-hundred-thirty-seven, Revision two, section three point two" | U.S. government work, public domain, safe to quote verbatim. States that Categorize exists to determine adverse impact from loss of confidentiality, integrity, and availability. | The exact three-part question you just asked about CAPA records, access across sites, and audit-log availability during an assessment. |
| NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Ch. 2 (Figure 2 framing — Select) | "...Chapter Two" | Same tier. States that Select means choosing an initial control set and tailoring it to reduce risk to an acceptable level, based on an assessment of risk. | What you'll use to size the eQMS's control set to whatever Categorize decides, instead of copying a generic checklist. |

## The actual text

The Categorize step's own purpose statement — already named once in the last module, applied here
for the first time — quoted verbatim from `sources/nist/sp-800-37r2-excerpt.md`:

> The purpose of the Categorize step is to inform organizational risk management processes and
> tasks by determining the adverse impact to organizational operations and assets, individuals,
> other organizations, and the Nation with respect to the loss of confidentiality, integrity, and
> availability of organizational systems and the information processed, stored, and transmitted by
> those systems.

Strip "organizational operations and assets... other organizations, and the Nation" down to
Lakeshore's own scale — a private blood establishment has no "Nation" to answer to — and what's
left maps cleanly: adverse impact to Lakeshore's operations (a site that can't produce a record
during an assessment), its assets (the audit trail itself, which is the asset here), and
individuals (a donor, a patient, or an employee named in a CAPA record whose confidentiality
matters). That's the full weight of "loss of confidentiality, integrity, and availability" sized to
Lakeshore's actual world instead of a federal agency's.

Select's one-line action, quoted verbatim from the same excerpt (part of Figure 2's framing,
already quoted in full in the last module — this is the one line this module actually acts on):

> Select an initial set of controls for the system and tailor the controls as needed to reduce
> risk to an acceptable level based on an assessment of risk.

Two words in that sentence are doing real work and are easy to skim past. **"Initial"** means you
don't start from nothing and you don't start from a maximum-security template either — you start
from a baseline sized to the categorization you just made. **"Tailor"** means that baseline isn't
the final answer; you add, remove, or adjust controls based on what's actually true about the
eQMS, not what a generic checklist assumes.

## Reasoning to a categorization — not asserting one

Here's the actual decision, reasoned out instead of just stated. The eQMS holds CAPA records,
document control, and internal-audit logs across all three sites — records that don't just
document Lakeshore's quality system, they *are* the evidence an AABB assessor or FDA investigator
uses to judge whether Lakeshore's quality system is working. Walk the impact question through all
three again, this time asking "how bad, specifically":

- **Integrity failure** — an undetected alteration to a closed CAPA record isn't a local
  inconvenience. It's Lakeshore presenting evidence to a regulator or assessor that may no longer
  be true, without knowing it. That's a finding waiting to happen, and worse, a finding Lakeshore
  can't see coming because nothing caught the change.
- **Confidentiality failure** — exposure of an open CAPA record across sites, or to someone
  without a reason to see it, risks real harm to the people named in it and risks Lakeshore's own
  credibility if word gets out that its new centralizing system made records *less* protected than
  the patchwork it replaced.
- **Availability failure** — an audit log or document-control record unreachable during an active
  assessment isn't a technical hiccup. It reads, in the room, exactly like a missing record reads
  to an inspector: as if the record might not exist at all.

None of these three is "a inconvenience, recoverable with an apology." Each one plausibly produces
a real regulatory or AABB-facing consequence across all three sites at once, because the eQMS is
the single shared system of record for all of them. That's the actual reasoning, not a reflex,
for categorizing the eQMS as a **moderate-impact** system — not the lowest tier (a low-impact
system is one where loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability would have only limited
consequence, which doesn't describe data an assessor relies on to judge a closed-loop quality
process) and arguably a candidate for high-impact in a security-first shop, but moderate is the
defensible call here specifically because the eQMS's worst plausible failure is serious regulatory
and reputational exposure, not loss of life or an organization-ending event the way a true
high-impact clinical or product-release system would carry. The honest caveat: this is Lakeshore's
own reasoned judgment, not a number handed down by a standard — a different, equally careful
reviewer could reasonably argue for high-impact instead, given how central the eQMS now is to all
three sites' regulatory story. What would actually change that answer is a scope decision you
haven't made yet, not a fact you're missing: if the eQMS later becomes the sole system of record
with no other place a given CAPA or audit entry exists, that single-point-of-failure shift would
be real grounds to revisit the categorization upward.

## Selecting and tailoring a control set sized to that

Moderate-impact earns the eQMS a more substantial starting baseline than a low-impact system would
get, but tailoring — not maximalism — is still the job. This is where your systems administrator's
opening-scene instinct ("I'll make sure the usual people have the usual access") gets replaced with
something that would actually survive an assessor's question six months from now.

NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 itself, in the discussion of common controls the saved excerpt captures,
names **control families** as the organizing concept — groupings of related controls defined in
the separate control catalog, SP 800-53 (not independently fetched by this curriculum, so no
specific numbered control gets invented here — only the family names the saved excerpt itself
names). Three families map directly onto the three failure modes you just reasoned through:

- **Account and identity management** — who gets eQMS access, at what level, reviewed on what
  schedule, across all three sites. This is the direct answer to your systems administrator's
  original worry and to the confidentiality question: a named process for granting, reviewing, and
  revoking access, replacing "the usual people" with a documented list and a documented review
  date.
- **Audit** (logging) — a record of who changed what CAPA, document-control, or audit-log entry,
  and when. This is the direct answer to the integrity question: not preventing every possible
  alteration, but making sure an alteration can't happen *undetected*, which is the actual phrase
  in Categorize's purpose statement.
- **Physical and environmental protection** — controls over wherever the eQMS's underlying
  infrastructure actually sits, whatever that turns out to be for Lakeshore. This is the
  availability-side family worth naming explicitly, because the opening scenario's third question
  — the system down during an active assessment — is as much about where and how reliably the
  eQMS runs as it is about access.

Tailoring means Lakeshore doesn't adopt every control in all three families at maximum strength
just because the categorization came back moderate. It means the Director and the QA (and the
systems administrator, since account and identity management is squarely his domain) look at each
family and ask: given what moderate-impact actually means for *this* system, which controls in
this family earn their cost, and which would be theater? That tailoring conversation — not a
checklist copied from a lower-stakes system, and not a maximum-security build the eQMS doesn't
need — is Select's real output.

## What a reviewer would actually look for

No external body audits Lakeshore against RMF, the same honest note the last module made. What a
competent reviewer — your CIO, an AABB assessor who happens to ask, or you yourself revisiting
this later — would actually want to find is a short, dated record answering four questions: what
did Lakeshore decide the eQMS's impact level was, who decided it, what reasoning supported that
decision (not just the number), and which control families were selected and tailored because of
it. A bad answer sounds like "we figured moderate was about right" with no reasoning attached. A
good answer sounds like the walkthrough above — three named failure modes, a stated reason for
landing on moderate rather than low or high, and controls that trace back to specific failure
modes instead of a generic list.

## Common traps

**"Categorize is about how technically complex the system is."** No — it's about *impact if it
fails*, not complexity. A simple system holding records that drive major regulatory decisions can
categorize higher than a complicated system holding nothing anyone outside IT cares about.
Complexity is an implementation concern for the next module; impact is the only question
Categorize asks.

**"Once we picked moderate, the control list is fixed."** The Select step's own verb is "tailor,"
not "apply." A moderate-impact starting baseline is exactly that — a starting point. The real work
is the conversation about which controls in each family the eQMS actually needs, not treating a
baseline as a checkbox exercise.

## What this means for your job

- **Ask "which of the three — confidentiality, integrity, availability — are we actually worried
  about" whenever someone proposes a new control for the eQMS.** A control that doesn't trace back
  to a named impact is a control nobody has actually justified yet.
- **Expect your systems administrator's account-and-identity-management work to now have a
  written review schedule, not an informal one.** That's the direct, traceable fix for his
  opening-scene "I'll keep an eye on it" from the last module — ask to see the schedule, not just
  hear that one exists.
- **Push your QA and your administrator to agree on the categorization together, not separately.**
  Confidentiality and availability concerns tend to surface from IT-operations instincts;
  integrity concerns tend to surface from quality instincts. The eQMS needs both in the room for
  Categorize to actually work.
- **Watch for the two failure modes in either direction.** A categorization that's quietly lower
  than the evidence supports (because nobody wants to justify more controls) is as much a finding
  as a maximal control list nobody can explain the cost of.
- **Keep saying this is Lakeshore's own methodology, not a requirement, every time you make this
  decision out loud** — it's an easy thing for a new team member to start repeating as "the rule"
  rather than "our choice," and the distinction matters the next time someone asks why Lakeshore
  did this at all.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your systems administrator asks, "Does categorizing the eQMS as moderate-impact mean NIST or some federal body is now reviewing how we run it?" What do you tell him?

No. Categorize is a step inside RMF, a structure Lakeshore adopted voluntarily as its own internal
methodology — no federal body reviews, approves, or has any legal standing over how a private
blood establishment categorizes or runs an internal system. The "moderate-impact" label is
Lakeshore's own reasoned judgment, recorded for Lakeshore's own later reference, not a
classification submitted to or reviewed by anyone outside the organization.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Your Quality Analyst asks why the eQMS wasn't categorized as low-impact, since "nothing about a document-control system sounds dangerous." How do you answer?

Low-impact would mean loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability has only limited
consequence — and that's not true here. An undetected alteration to a closed CAPA record, exposure
of an in-progress CAPA across sites, or an unreachable audit log during an active AABB assessment
each plausibly produces a real regulatory or reputational consequence, because the eQMS is the
shared system of record feeding decisions at all three sites. "Sounds dangerous" isn't the test —
"how bad is the realistic worst case" is, and the realistic worst case here is serious, even though
nobody's safety is directly at stake the way it would be for a true high-impact clinical system.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: A peer mentions their organization picked specific NIST SP 800-53 control numbers for their own system, like a numbered access-control requirement. Should Lakeshore do the same for the eQMS?

Not based on anything built in this course. SP 800-53 is the actual control catalog with specific
numbered controls, and this curriculum has never independently fetched or verified that document
— only named "control families" as a concept, drawn from what SP 800-37 itself references. Citing
a specific control number Lakeshore never actually looked up would be inventing a citation, exactly
the mistake this curriculum's sourcing discipline exists to prevent. Naming the family (account and
identity management, audit, physical and environmental protection) and reasoning about it in
Lakeshore's own terms is the honest, defensible version of this work without that source.
:::

## Where this goes next

Categorize named the impact level; Select named and tailored the control families that answer it.
Neither step asked whether those controls actually get built correctly or whether anyone
independent checked that they work — that's `implement-and-assess-controls`, picking up exactly
where the tailoring conversation above leaves off.
